en: The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, when the hour had come, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.

As these many bhikṣus were entering the city of Śrāvastī for alms, they heard that outside the palace gate of King Prasenajit there was a great multitude of people, each holding hands, weeping and wailing, and saying this:

"In this land there is a great and wicked bandit named Aṅgulimāla; he slays the people with such cruelty that he has no heart of compassion. Villages can find no peace, cities find no peace, and the people find no peace."
He murders the people, taking a finger from each to fashion a flower-tufted topknot; for this reason he is named Aṅgulimāla. I pray that Your Majesty will subdue this man.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having finished their almsround in Śrāvastī, put away their robes and bowls after their meal, washed their hands and feet, placed their sitting mats (niṣadana) over their shoulders, and went to where the World-Honored One was; there they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"We, many bhikṣus, having dressed in our robes and taken up our bowls at the proper time, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food."
He then heard that outside the palace gate of King Kūbara, a great multitude of people were weeping with hands clasped together, saying:

"In our realm there is a great bandit named Aṅgulimāla; he slaughters the people and takes a finger from each one to fashion a flower-garland for his hair. For this reason he is called Aṅgulimāla; we pray that you will subdue him."
When the World-Honored One heard this from the bhikṣu, he rose from his seat and, as Aṅgulimāla was staying in three locations, the World-Honored One proceeded to those places.
At that time, there were people carrying firewood and grass, farmers working in their fields, and travelers who approached the World-Honored One and said to him:
"Sramana, do not travel by this path."

The reason for this is that within this path there was Aṅgulimāla, who slaughtered people and lacked any compassion for sentient beings; he brought harm to cities, towns, and villages alike, and he made flower garlands from the fingers of those he killed.

He harassed the World-Honored One such that any group of recluses or commoners traveling along this road had to pass only after ten people gathered together; or twenty, or thirty, or forty, or fifty, or a hundred, or even a thousand people had to gather before they could pass.
"Aṅgulimāla will take whatever he desires from his heart and eat it.
Then the World-Honored One proceeded forward, with no intention of turning back.
When Aṅgulimāla saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar, having seen him, he thought to himself:
“Whenever people desire to pass along this road, ten must gather together, or even a thousand, before they may pass; then, according to their will, they slaughter them.”
"However, this śramaṇa has come alone without a companion; I shall now seize and kill him.
At that moment, Aṅgulimāla drew the sword from his waist and went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw Aṅgulimāla approaching from afar and turned back along the same path.
Then Aṅgulimāla pursued the World-Honored One, exerting all his strength and power in an attempt to catch up with him, yet he could not reach him.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla thought to himself:

"I can overtake elephants, and I can catch up with horses, and I can catch up with chariots, and I can catch up with fierce bulls, and I can catch up with men; yet this śramaṇa’s pace is not even swift, and though I exert all my strength and power, I cannot catch him."
Then, Aṅgulimāla called out from afar to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
"O śramaṇa," the World-Honored One said,
"I have long remained abiding, yet you do not abide."
Then Aṅgulimāla spoke this verse:
“The śramaṇa acts as if he dwells, yet says that I do not dwell;
The śramaṇa explains this meaning: ‘I myself dwell, while you do not.’”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Aṅgulimāla:
"Listen to what I say; I abide in the meaning of that in which you do not abide.
He then spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One always abides in himself, and all receive his grace;
yet you harbor a murderous intent and do not avoid evil conduct.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla thought to himself:
"Am I now performing evil deeds?
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke this verse:
"The śramaṇa has uttered this verse, Having given rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward me."
Immediately casting aside his waist-sword, he prostrated with his five limbs in homage to the Buddha.
Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he requested to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said, "Come, bhikṣu," and he was immediately ordained into full precepts.
It is the constant law of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak these words:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!"

Immediately, his hair and beard fell off of their own accord as if he had been shaved; after seven days had passed, whatever robes he wore—whether they were of the finest fine silk, or of cotton, or of *karpāsa*, or of *dukūla*—were transformed into monastic robes (*kāṣāya*).
After the Blessed One had spoken thus: "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
"You should practice the holy life within my Dharma; with a mind free from conceit, you shall bring an end to the very root of suffering.
At that moment, Aṅgulimāla’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and he stood behind the World-Honored One, clad in the saffron robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking behind Aṅgulimāla, proceeding from the Śālavana Garden to the Jeta Grove, where he took his seat.

Then, Aṅgulimāla was instructed by the venerable elder bhikṣus in matters of deportment and ritual propriety. Having received this instruction, he thought: "For what reason do sons of noble family, with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Way and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life? To reach the end of the source of birth and death; the holy life having been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and one shall no longer receive a mother’s womb."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla became an arhat.

Then, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla practiced the forest-dweller’s life in uninhabited places; he always went on almsrounds without discriminating between households and wore the fivefold patched robe, which others find disadvantageous.
At that time, King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army; having assembled the fourfold army, he departed from the city of Śrāvastī, intending to go and kill the bandit Aṅgulimāla.
Then, King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"I should first go to the place where the World-Honored One is and explain this matter in detail to him; if the World-Honored One gives instructions, I shall carry them out."
At that time, King Prasenajit approached the Jeta Grove on foot and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Now, there are five characteristics of a Kṣatriya royal lineage. What are these five?

Having set aside his parasol, celestial crown, vermilion fly-whisk handle, sword-jewel, and sandals, he placed them all at one side, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and sat down to one side.
When King Prasenajit had finished sitting, the World-Honored One asked him:
"For what reason has the King assembled the fourfold army and come to my dwelling with dust covering his robes?"
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"In this city of Śrāvastī there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla who slaughters people without any heart of compassion. Both the cities and the villages loathe him; the populace is scattered and divided. After he has slaughtered people, he takes their fingers to fashion a flower-garland for his hair."
"I wish to go and kill that man.
The World-Honored One said,

"If the King were now to see Aṅgulimāla with his hair and beard shaven, wearing the three dharma-robes, having left the household life out of firm faith to study the Way— what would the King do with him?"
The king replied:
"What would you have me take?
I shall inquire after his welfare, pay him homage, serve him, and make offerings to him; I shall harbor no harmful intent toward him."
"But, World-Honored One,
how could those cruel people, who have no heart of compassion for sentient beings, be able to cultivate the practice of a śramaṇa?"
At that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was seated cross-legged not far from the World-Honored One, with his body erect and his mind upright, fixing his attention before him.
Then the World-Honored One raised his right hand, pointing toward where Aṅgulimāla was, and said: "Great King!
"This is the bandit Aṅgulimāla.
When King Prasenajit saw Aṅgulimāla, he was seized with terror and his hair stood on end.
Then the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
“Great King! Do not harbor fear; go yourself to that place, and he will speak with you himself.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit went to the place where Aṅgulimāla was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at his feet and stood to one side.
At that time, King Prasenajit asked Aṅgulimāla,
"Venerable Aṅgulimāla, what is your name now? Aṅgulimāla replied:
“Great King! My name is Gāgū, and my mother’s name is Mandāyanī.
The king replied:

“Exert yourself well for your own sake; I shall now provide for the Venerable Gāgga as long as I live with robes, almsfood, medicine for sickness, and bedding and seating, without any stinginess, and I shall always protect him with the Dharma.”
Then King Prasenajit prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and approached the World-Honored One; having prostrated himself at his feet, he sat to one side.
Then King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“World-Honored One, those who have not been subdued, you are able to subdue them. The Tathāgata causes all who are stubborn and fierce to submit, yet he subdues sentient beings without the use of swords or staves.”
"I have many matters to attend to and wish to return to my kingdom.
The World-Honored One said, "Now is precisely the right time; do as you desire."
Then King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla, on that very day, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, while Aṅgulimāla was begging for alms, he saw a woman who was pregnant and on the verge of giving birth but had not yet done so; having seen her, he thought to himself:
"This sentient being is suffering greatly."

At that time, Aṅgulimāla entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. After his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and went to where the World-Honored One was; there he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.
Then Aṅgulimāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Just now, having put on my robes and taken up my bowl, I entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
While begging, I saw a woman who was pregnant and about to give birth, yet she could not deliver in due time. Having seen this, I thought to myself:"
"These classes of sentient beings are undergoing great suffering.
The World-Honored One said: "You!..."
Aṅgulimāla went to that woman and said to her:
"O noble lady, since my birth from a noble womb, I do not recall ever having taken the life of a living being. By this word of truth, may you give birth safely."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Is it not the case that I have spoken falsely to you?
For this reason: within this very body, I have slaughtered countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."
The World-Honored One said:
"When you were in the secular world, your current status as a noble one is not the same as it was before.
Pointing to your topknot, enter the city of Śrāvastī and make this proclamation in the streets and alleys:"
"Virtuous ones, you should protect five things. What are these five?
Refraining from killing, refraining from taking what is not given, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, and refraining from drinking intoxicants."

The reason for this is that the retribution for killing is to receive the retribution of a blade for having given a blade; the retribution for stealing is increased poverty; the retribution for sexual misconduct is that one’s wife becomes increasingly adulterous; the retribution for lying is that the breath of sentient beings becomes foul and putrid; and the retribution for drinking alcohol is increased disorder among the multitude.
He went to where the woman was, and having arrived, he said to her:
"Since my birth from the Noble One, I have never recalled killing or harming any living being; by this word of truth, may the woman give birth safely."
He replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One. Then,
at the proper time, Aṅgulimāla put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
He made this proclamation throughout the streets and alleys:
"Virtuous ones, you should protect [women] in five matters until they have safely given birth.
Gradually, he proceeded to where that woman was.
Having arrived, he said to the woman:
"Since my birth from the Noble Ones, I do not recall ever having taken the life of a single person; by this word of truth, may you, O woman, give birth in safety."
When Aṅgulimāla had finished speaking these words, that woman immediately gave birth.
Then, after his meal, Aṅgulimāla wished to depart from the city of Śrāvastī.
One person struck the finger-tuft and body with a stone; another struck the finger-tuft and body with a staff; and yet another cut the finger-tuft and body with a sword until it was mangled.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla, his head split open and his body covered in blood, left the city of Śrāvastī and went to where the World-Honored One was.
When the World-Honored One saw Aṅgulimāla approaching from afar—his head split and dripping with blood, staining his saṃghāṭī robe, and his body wounded—he spoke to him, saying:

"Endure this; do not give rise to evil thoughts. For the retribution of such conduct, you shall enter hell for countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas; what you are experiencing now is not even worth mentioning."
Then Aṅgulimāla said to the Buddha: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! So it is, Tathāgata!
Then, with a heart of harmony and joy, Aṅgulimāla spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"My forbearance is most firm and steadfast, with no heart of increase or decrease;
having now heard the True Dharma, I am therefore free from indolence and pride.
My hearing of the Dharma is likewise steadfast; I delight in faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
By drawing near to virtuous friends, one is able to discern all phenomena.
In the past, I was an evil bandit named Aṅgulimāla,
who was swept away and drowned by the waters.
Returning to my own refuge, I take refuge in the Dharma;
having distinguished the Dharma and attained the three types of supernormal knowledge, I have returned to the station of the Buddhas.
Formerly, I practiced heedlessness and took the lives of many beings.
Now called one of ultimate sincerity and truth, he no longer harms or kills others.
In the actions of body and speech, his mind likewise harbors no malice;
such a person is called a "slayer," yet he is not envied by others.
Even a young bhikṣu who conforms to the Buddha’s precepts illuminates this world,
like the moon when clouds and mist have vanished.
Having previously engaged in lustful excesses, he later reforms and does not transgress again.
This illuminates the world, like the moon when clouds and mist have vanished.
Though swept away by the waters, it remains as firm as tempered steel.
As a skilled craftsman follows the grain of the wood, so does the wise person cultivate their own body.
Whether they are struck with blades and staves, Or whipped with whips, halters, and traces,
Being without strength and without support, They are subdued by the Buddha.
Neither do they desire death, Nor do they desire life.
"Observe for yourself the proper timing; remain composed and do not be impulsive.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing Raṭṭhapāla, addressed the bhikṣus:

"Do you see among the bhikṣus one such as my disciple who possesses swift intelligence and understands the Dharma upon hearing it—namely, the bhikṣu Gāgga, who understands the Dharma upon hearing it?"
The bhikṣus said: “No, World-Honored One!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the bhikṣu Aṅgirasa is the foremost in swift wisdom."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Aṅgulimāla Spoken by the Buddha.
